post1.text:
Most companies don't stall at $50M because of bad strategy. They stall because the leader who got them there is not the leader who can take them further.

That's the uncomfortable truth scaling companies avoid until it costs them.

Recent moves by growth-stage companies show a clear pattern: firms that successfully scale past major revenue thresholds are making deliberate, structural leadership changes before the pressure forces them to. They're not reacting. They're building ahead of the curve.

Here's what that looks like in practice:

First, founders and CEOs must separate their identity from their operating role. The skills that built the company are rarely the skills that scale it.

Second, leadership capacity has to grow before revenue does, not after. Hiring executives reactively is one of the most expensive mistakes a $50M company can make.

Third, culture at scale is not what you say. It's what you tolerate under pressure.

The leaders who understand this early create the headroom to grow. The ones who don't become the ceiling.

What's the hardest leadership assumption you've had to let go of as your company grew?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. Buffini and Company just added three senior executives specifically to scale their coaching operations.

That's a deliberate, structural move and it's exactly what growth-stage companies get wrong when they wait too long to make it.

Here's Autobahn's take: companies in the $50M to $500M range often underbuild their leadership bench precisely when revenue growth makes it feel unnecessary. Then scaling pressure arrives and they're scrambling to hire and integrate senior talent at the worst possible moment.

Buffini's approach signals something important. Leadership infrastructure is not a reward for growth. It's a prerequisite for it.

If you're navigating a similar inflection point, this is worth a read.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMicEFVX3lxTE80SmJLNXdFS1VDcE9QNXQ2YzNFUDNUSzItcWljNWEyb2NEUVJ0UzdweEIzaVZyclAyWk5fcW54Nlo2U21GSVVoMHFJaVpLSFdaMU1tMXRIWU8wMTJvc3RJNTM5VkhoaVFxZnZFM0VlWVU

post3.text:
Buffini and Company recently hired three senior executives to scale their coaching business. Smart move. And it reflects a principle that Katherine Slain writes about directly in Chapter 1 of our new book.

The chapter is called Lead Like Lives Depend On It. The title is intentional.

Katherine's core argument is that leadership at scale is not a softer, more refined version of early-stage hustle. It requires a completely different posture, and most leaders don't make that shift until damage is already done.

One insight she surfaces early: the moment your company's growth outpaces your leadership development, you're not scaling anymore. You're borrowing time.

There's a framework in this chapter that helps leaders identify exactly where that gap is opening up before it becomes a crisis.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: The leader who built your $50M company may be the single biggest obstacle to your $500M company. That's not a criticism. It's a structural reality that most scaling businesses discover too late. Leadership has to grow ahead of revenue, not chase it. Here's what that actually requires and why so few companies get it right.

post1.text:
Most business owners optimize for growth. Almost none optimize for value. Those are not the same thing.

A company doing $50M in revenue can sell for wildly different multiples depending on factors that have nothing to do with top-line performance. Buyer concentration risk, management dependency, and recurring revenue mix matter far more than most founders realize until it is too late to fix them.

Entrepreneur recently highlighted how founders consistently underestimate how early exit planning needs to start. The owners who command the highest multiples begin preparing three to five years before they intend to sell, not three to five months.

Here is what that preparation actually looks like at the $50M+ level:

1. Clean up your customer concentration. No single client should represent more than 15% of revenue.
2. Build a leadership team that can operate without you. Buyers price out key-person risk aggressively.
3. Know your EBITDA adjustments cold. Sellers who cannot defend their add-backs leave money on the table.

If you sold your business tomorrow, would the number surprise you?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank walks through the core business exit strategies available to owners, from strategic sales to management buyouts to family succession. It is a solid overview, but it stops short of addressing the issue that trips up most scaling companies.

Knowing your options is not the same as knowing which option maximizes your outcome.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, the gap between a good exit and a great one is usually not the type of deal structure chosen. It is the preparation done two to four years before any deal is on the table. Recurring revenue, management depth, and clean financials do more for your multiple than any late-stage negotiation tactic.

Read the J.P. Morgan piece as a starting point, then ask yourself whether your business is actually ready for any of those paths.

post3.text:
Entrepreneur recently made a point that resonates deeply with us: founders spend years building their companies and almost no time engineering a valuable exit. By the time most owners think about selling, the window to improve their multiple has already closed.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this head-on. The chapter is titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, and it was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, two practitioners who have worked through these transactions from both sides of the table.

One thing Paul and George make clear: your multiple is not set by market conditions. It is set by decisions you make years in advance. The businesses that consistently command premium valuations are not the fastest-growing ones. They are the most deliberately prepared ones.

There is a specific framework in this chapter that changes how owners think about value creation. We will leave the details for the book.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

The difference between a good outcome and a great one rarely comes down to deal structure or market timing. It comes down to how intentionally you built the business before any buyer ever showed up.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because the execution never had a real owner.

Forbes recently broke down the core reasons leadership teams fall apart at strategy execution. The pattern is familiar: the plan looks sharp in the boardroom, then quietly dies in the calendar.

Here is what mid-market leaders at the $50M-plus stage need to understand:

1. Strategy without a cadence is just aspiration. Execution requires weekly rhythms, not quarterly reviews.

2. Accountability has to live with a person, not a department. Diffused ownership is no ownership.

3. The gap between planning and execution widens exactly when companies are scaling fastest. Growth adds complexity faster than most leadership teams adapt.

Companies that make the leap from $50M to $500M are not smarter planners. They are relentless executors. They build systems that outlast any single leader or initiative.

So here is the real question: Does your leadership team know the difference between approving a plan and actually running one?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SmartBrief laid out a practical framework for building a plan-execution process that actually produces results, not just slide decks.

It is worth reading, especially if your company is growing fast.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M, and this is one of the most consistent failure points we see. Leaders invest heavily in building the plan. They underinvest almost entirely in the system that runs it day to day.

The companies that scale successfully treat execution as a discipline, not a follow-up item. That means defined owners, visible metrics, and a cadence the whole leadership team is accountable to.

If your current strategic plan has no clear execution owner and no weekly rhythm attached to it, start there.

Read the full SmartBrief piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMimAFBVV95cUxNRk8xX0ZPak91anhUdC1rSXY5X2FVMnBhb1J6bUFsT2VVdU5KbXhFNDRRaEdvMkk5M0EwVU5qajdsRHFlOVlINWZDckE3UE1pQ2xHdGFuTzBiSm9BNURLMDV3NnJHWU1zNlRQa1Q3MlREVFFPd2VCUWJtTWk0VTZfRTJDd09WenJMQ0hiQzJlNXpab1VNSVdkbQ?oc=5

post3.text:
Strategic planning gets a lot of attention. Execution gets a lot of blame. Rarely do companies take a hard look at the space in between.

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on real experience across wildly different industries to make a simple but powerful point: the business that scales is not the one with the best-looking plan. It is the one that builds a repeatable system for following through.

They share what they discovered working with companies at the $50M-plus stage, where the stakes get higher and the old habits of running a smaller business quietly start working against you.

If you think your team has a strategy problem, you might actually have an execution problem in disguise.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

At the $50M-plus stage, execution stops being a follow-up and starts being a discipline. Here is what separates the leadership teams that scale from the ones that stall.

post1.text:
Most companies between $50M and $500M do not have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There is a difference. Habits are what your team does when no one is looking. Strategy is what your team does when the market gets hard.

Recent research from McKinsey confirms what we see constantly with scaling companies: the gap between B2B winners and everyone else is not product quality or pricing. It is a disciplined, deliberate approach to how revenue gets created and protected.

Here is what that actually looks like in practice:

First, your ideal customer profile needs to be narrow enough to be useful. Vague targeting is not a strategy, it is hope.

Second, your sales motion has to match your buyer's decision process, not your internal org chart.

Third, accountability structures inside the sales team cannot be optional. Either there are consequences or there are not.

Every day a growing company operates without these three things in place, it is leaving real revenue on the table.

What is the one thing your sales team does consistently that you cannot actually explain why?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Gartner makes a critical point: the time AI saves your sales reps will not automatically convert into more revenue. Without deliberate intervention from sales leadership, that recovered time gets absorbed into low-value activity.

This matters enormously for companies scaling past $50M. At that stage, you are not just managing a sales team, you are building a sales system. Technology without strategy is just expensive noise.

The companies winning right now are the ones whose leaders are actively deciding how recaptured time gets redeployed, into higher-quality conversations, better pipeline management, and sharper account focus.

If you are adopting AI tools in your sales org, the first question is not what the tool does. It is what your people will do differently because of it.

Read the full Gartner piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYEFVX3lxTE83YmJZYVNxUUtqV1lJanRha3hGWnFtdjJYSm5FWURzTUFrVm1uTDB2R1VRWklWVlM4cVhURDNTMVFxVmw0Ql9YZUZrdndhcC1JWFRZczVJRmxlR1REQmVvMg

post3.text:
Bain and Company recently published research on what separates B2B growth winners from companies that plateau. The findings point directly at something our authors Deb and Brandon write about in Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business: Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation.

The title is not a metaphor. It is math.

Deb and Brandon work with companies in the $50M to $500M range who believe they have a sales strategy when what they actually have is a collection of individual rep behaviors held together by optimism. The chapter lays out a framework for turning that into something repeatable and scalable.

The one thing we will tease: the problem almost never starts with the sales team. It starts one level above them.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most B2B companies at the $50M mark are not losing revenue because of bad salespeople. They are losing it because no one ever built an actual sales strategy. New research from McKinsey and Bain confirms the gap between scaling winners and everyone else is structural, not personal. Here is what that means for your business right now.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost strategy disguised as ambition.

Companies scaling past $50M tend to make the same mistake: they treat headcount as a proxy for progress. More bodies, more output. Except that math stops working fast.

SHRM's recent research on 2026 hiring trends confirms what the best operators already know. The companies pulling ahead are not hiring at greater volume. They are hiring with greater precision, matching roles to specific growth outcomes rather than filling org chart boxes.

Three things worth internalizing if you are running a company in this range:

1. Define the job the role needs to do before you write the job description. Most leaders skip this step entirely.

2. Your top performers are already telling you what great looks like. Few companies actually study that data.

3. A bad hire at the director level does not cost you one salary. It costs you a year of momentum.

So here is the real question: Is your hiring process built to find the right person, or just to find a person fast?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM on 2026 hiring trends makes a point that scaling companies cannot afford to ignore: precision in hiring now matters more than speed or volume.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Companies between $50M and $200M often have recruiting processes built for a smaller, scrappier version of themselves. Those processes do not scale. They produce noise, not signal.

The fix is not a new ATS or a fancier job board. It is clarity on what each role actually needs to accomplish in the next 12 months, and the discipline to hold that line through the interview process.

If your talent acquisition strategy still looks like it did when you were a $20M company, it is time to rebuild it. We can help.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aE0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring is not new to us. It is central to Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business.

The chapter is called The Talent Engine, written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West. Together they lay out what separates companies that scale their people strategy from those that just scale their payroll.

One of the ideas they surface early: most mid-market companies have a talent acquisition process, but very few have a talent engine. The difference is not semantics. An engine is designed, measured, and tuned. A process is just a habit nobody has questioned yet.

If your company is growing revenue but your org feels like it is straining under the weight of that growth, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at the $50M+ level are not suffering from a lack of data. They are drowning in it. Hootsuite recently published a list of 31 social media metrics alone worth tracking in 2026. Thirty-one. For one channel.

Here is what we see consistently with scaling companies:

First, when every metric is a priority, none of them are. Leadership alignment collapses when the scorecard has 40 lines.

Second, the metrics that get tracked are often the ones that are easy to pull, not the ones that actually predict performance. Vanity beats clarity every time if you let it.

Third, the companies that scale successfully tend to shrink their dashboards before they grow their revenue. Fewer numbers, owned by specific people, reviewed on a cadence that drives action.

The question is not what you should be measuring. It is what you would stop measuring if you had to cut your KPIs in half tomorrow.

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite outlines 30 financial metrics and KPIs worth tracking as you head into 2026. It is a solid reference, and the list is comprehensive.

But here is the tension we see with scaling companies: comprehensive is not the same as actionable.

When a business is growing from $50M toward $500M, the financial metrics that matter most are the ones tied directly to the decisions on your calendar this quarter. Not every ratio on a best-practices list.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams to identify the five to seven financial indicators that actually govern their growth model, and build accountability around those instead of around a spreadsheet that impresses auditors.

If your team cannot recite your top KPIs without opening a dashboard, you have too many. Read the full article here and ask yourself which five on that list you would actually act on: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikwFBVV95cUxNcThuZllxNkVka0dpOV9QdHZQM2RiU0tfMGVIR05tdW9ZN1AtYngwQ1d4WDFSb3ZNSUxKNHFCSUR4aC1lR1g2ZWYzWFE0NWF1WmVpejAxOW9VRFdJa01yLUFKa1hvbjNGQnR6a2hZcVVtQzgwRXNCdXVGbjhfNWR2eWpTSlFyRk5zLVZ3MnJvMU14ZjA

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every leadership team running a growing company needs to read before their next quarterly planning session.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is called Death by KPIs. It was written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, and it addresses something most scaling companies get wrong: the belief that more measurement equals more control.

One insight the chapter surfaces is that KPI overload does not just slow down reporting. It actively undermines the accountability structures you need to grow. When everyone owns everything, no one owns anything.

As tools for tracking metrics multiply and lists like Business.com's 14 KPI platforms keep growing, the real competitive advantage is knowing which numbers to ignore.

Rock Your Business, the second book from Autobahn Consultants by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, is available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most scaling companies do not have a data problem. They have a focus problem. When your leadership team is tracking 40 KPIs across six dashboards, you are not managing performance, you are managing noise. The companies that successfully grow from $50M to $500M share one counterintuitive habit: they measure less, and they mean it.

post1.text:
Most companies are measuring AI adoption wrong. They track usage rates and rollout timelines. They should be tracking the gap between what leadership believes is happening and what employees actually experience.

Recent reporting from The New York Times found that CEOs consistently rate their AI rollouts as successful while employees tell a very different story. That disconnect is not a communication problem. It is a strategy problem.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

1. AI adoption without workflow redesign creates the illusion of progress. Tools get deployed. Habits do not change.

2. Productivity gains from AI are real, but they rarely convert to revenue growth automatically. That conversion requires deliberate leadership decisions, not software subscriptions.

3. The companies winning with AI right now are treating it as an operational model shift, not a technology upgrade.

If your leadership team believes the rollout is going well, when did you last ask the people doing the actual work?

#AIStrategy #ScalingBusiness #OperationalExcellence

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fast Company Middle East surfaced something worth sitting with: AI is reliably boosting productivity, but CEOs are struggling to convert those efficiency gains into actual business growth.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is exactly where the risk lives. You invest in AI tools, your team gets faster, and then... the revenue line does not move the way you expected. The productivity gain gets absorbed rather than redirected.

The missing piece is almost always intentional redeployment. Faster workflows only create growth when leadership actively decides what to do with the time and capacity that gets freed up. That decision does not happen by default.

If your team is more productive but your top line is not reflecting it, that is a strategy conversation, not a technology conversation.

post1.text:
The leaders who never doubt themselves are the ones you should worry about.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a flaw to fix. It isn't. Research increasingly shows that the self-questioning it produces is actually a signal of high standards and sharp situational awareness. Leaders who feel it tend to listen harder, check their assumptions more carefully, and stay open to being wrong.

For executives scaling a company past $50M, that matters more than confidence does. Here is why:

1. Overconfidence at scale kills companies. The leader who thinks they have all the answers stops building teams that challenge them.

2. Doubt, when channeled, drives diligence. The exec who questions whether they belong in the room often prepares better than the one who assumes they own it.

3. Self-awareness is a competitive advantage. At this stage of growth, your blind spots cost more than your competitors do.

The question is not how to eliminate imposter syndrome. It is whether you know how to use it.

What is the internal doubt you keep suppressing that might actually be telling you something useful?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fast Company makes a case worth sitting with: embracing imposter syndrome, rather than fighting it, is what separates good leaders from great ones.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M. The leaders who struggle most are rarely the ones who doubt themselves. They are the ones who stopped doubting themselves too soon.

Growth at that level demands a specific kind of humility. New markets, new org structures, new talent requirements. The executives who treat uncertainty as a prompt to learn, rather than a threat to hide, build companies that can actually handle the pressure of scale.

If you are navigating a growth inflection point, read this one. It is short and it is worth your time.

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it asks exactly the question most executives avoid.

Authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, this chapter goes straight at imposter syndrome in senior leadership, not to dismiss it, and not to celebrate it, but to help leaders understand what it is actually telling them at the specific pressure points of scaling a business.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the feeling of not belonging in the room is not a bug in high-performing leaders. It shows up at the exact moments when the stakes are highest and the old playbook stops working.

post1.text:
The best-run $50M+ companies we work with share one uncomfortable truth: their leaders have no plan for their own lives.

They have strategic plans. Financial models. Succession frameworks. But ask a founder what they want their life to look like in five years, and you get silence.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this plain: founders obsess over growth trajectories but almost never design the life those trajectories are supposed to fund.

Here is what that costs you at scale:

1. Burnout disguised as busyness becomes a cultural export. Your team mirrors your pace, not your words.

2. Major decisions, including acquisitions, exits, and hires, get made reactively because there is no personal filter to run them through.

3. The company grows. The leader shrinks. That gap eventually shows up in the business results.

Life planning is not soft. It is the operating system underneath every business decision you make.

So here is the real question: if your business hit $500M tomorrow, would you actually know what to do with the life that comes with it?

#LeadershipDevelopment #ScalingUp #BusinessStrategy

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur made a point that every founder at our level needs to sit with: almost no one plans for the exit with the same rigor they plan for growth.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Leaders scaling from $50M to $500M pour everything into the business, and nothing into designing what comes next for themselves personally.

That is not just a personal problem. It creates strategic problems. Leaders without a personal endgame make inconsistent decisions about capital, talent, and timing. The business feels it.

The fix is not complicated, but it does require intention. Start by asking what you actually want the business to do for your life, not just what you want the business to do.

Read the full article and then ask yourself if your exit plan is as sharp as your growth plan.
